analysis.one_liner: Requires electronics makers to share repair parts, tools, and manuals with independent repair shops and owners.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on February 5, 2026 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it awaits action with two Democratic cosponsors and no hearing or vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Repair Act would require companies that make digital electronics to sell or provide repair parts, tools, and service manuals to independent repair shops and to owners of the equipment, on the same terms they offer their own authorized repair network. It would also ban practices like "parts pairing," where software blocks a device from working properly unless the replacement part is manufacturer-approved, and bans on non-dismissible warning alerts about unofficial parts. Enforcement would fall to the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of phones, laptops, appliances, and other electronics who can now choose a cheaper independent repair instead of buying a replacement; independent repair shops, which gain access to the same parts and documentation as authorized providers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Device owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Requires original equipment manufacturers to make documentation, parts, and tools available to independent repair providers and owners on terms equal to the best terms they offer their own authorized repair network.

Bans parts pairing and similar mechanisms that block the installation of functional replacement parts, degrade device performance after independent repair, or display non-dismissible warnings about non-manufacturer parts.

Lets the Federal Trade Commission enforce the requirements as an unfair or deceptive practice and lets state attorneys general sue violators for penalties, restitution, and damages on behalf of state residents.
Covers equipment with security locks by requiring manufacturers to provide what is needed to disable and reset them during repair, rather than excluding such devices.

analysis.who_pays: Electronics and equipment manufacturers, which would lose control of their repair networks and some repair revenue, and would bear the cost of making parts, tools, and manuals available; some cost could be passed into device prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill bars manufacturers from being liable for damage, data loss, privacy breaches, or poor results from independent repairs, so owners who choose independent repair bear more of the risk themselves.

It exempts several large categories from the repair mandate entirely: motor vehicles, medical devices, off-road and non-road vehicles including aircraft and motorcycles, and emergency communications equipment.

Enforcement depends on FTC rulemaking and litigation, which can take years, and manufacturers may argue that repair options raise safety and data-security concerns for consumers who use unofficial parts or providers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would make repairing the devices people already own cheaper and more practical, and extend the useful life of electronics, while the main costs fall on manufacturers whose repair business and parts sales would face competition. Its main design weaknesses are the broad exclusions (most notably medical devices and vehicles) and the full liability shield for manufacturers over independent repairs, which shifts repair risk onto the owner rather than eliminating it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill is two days into its life: it was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it sits with no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Representative Joseph Morelle introduced the Fair Repair Act on February 5, 2026, joined by Representative Perez.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction; that is the only action recorded since.
It has two cosponsors, both House Democrats, and no committee action or floor vote has taken place.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No outcome yet; manufacturers keep the existing repair arrangements unless and until the bill moves, which a two-cosponsor bill referred to committee rarely does on its own.

for.name: Rep. Joseph Morelle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Repair Act and referred it to Energy and Commerce.

for.name: Rep. Perez
for.what_they_did: Joined Morelle as an original cosponsor at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: Only the sponsor and two Democratic cosponsors are on record so far, and no member has opposed it yet; right-to-repair proposals have drawn support from both parties in state legislatures, so the congressional split is not yet established.

industries.note: The bill requires them to sell parts, tools, and manuals to independent shops and owners on their most favorable authorized-network terms and bans parts pairing, cutting into manufacturer-controlled repair revenue. Ordinary owners gain cheaper repair options and longer device life.
They get legal access to the same parts, documentation, and tools as authorized repair networks, ending the disadvantage that pushes customers back to manufacturers.
The bill preserves existing authorized-provider arrangements, but those providers' advantage depends on exclusive access to parts and tools that the bill now opens to everyone.

analysis.trajectory: With two cosponsors, referral to Energy and Commerce, and no scheduled hearing or markup, the realistic path is that the bill sits in committee for the rest of the session unless right-to-repair is attached to a larger package or the cosponsor base grows sharply. Similar standalone repair bills introduced in past congresses have not reached the House floor.
